title: Markov Theory and Memory
content_html:
Markov Theory and Memory

A process is “Markov” if, given an appropriate description of the current state, the distribution of the future does not depend on the detailed past. Formally, the conditional distribution of the future given the present and past depends only on the present state. The Markov property is often misunderstood as “the system has no memory.” The more precise reading is: all relevant memory has been packed into the state variable. If the state is too small (e.g., it omits context), the model will fail; if the state is rich enough (e.g., it includes latent context or running summaries),

Markov dynamics can approximate genuinely history-dependent behavior. This makes Markov models attractive in cognitive science because they separate two design questions: (i) what is the right state representation, and (ii) what are the transition dynamics between states.

Markov chains as a language for “context drift” and forgetting

In a discrete-time Markov chain, transitions are described by a matrix of probabilities between states. Over time, many chains converge toward a stable long-run distribution (a “stationary distribution”) under standard conditions; the rate of convergence is characterized by a mixing time. If you interpret “state” as a coarse cognitive context (task mode, situation model, emotional/physiological regime), then:

  • Slow mixing corresponds to sticky contexts (strong persistence; slow context drift).
  • Fast mixing corresponds to rapidly changing contexts (weak persistence; rapid drift), which can resemble forgetting or interference when retrieval depends on reinstating context.

This is an interpretation: mixing time is a mathematical notion about convergence of distributions; the cognitive mapping is a modeling choice, not a claim that brains literally compute mixing times.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs): memory via latent states and event boundaries

HMMs treat observations as noisy emissions from an unobserved (latent) state sequence. In perception and memory, that latent state can represent which event you are currently in. A prominent example models event segmentation in continuous narrative data using an HMM-like structure, where each timepoint belongs to an event state and transitions correspond to event boundaries.

This reframes “remembering” as partly an inference problem: given sensory evidence, infer the current event state, and update only when evidence supports a boundary. Related work uses HMM-style approaches to identify event states across cortical hierarchies and timescales.

Successor representation: a Markov-friendly bridge between prediction and memory

In reinforcement learning, the successor representation (SR) represents a state by the expected discounted future occupancy of other states under a policy. SR was introduced as a way to improve generalization for temporal-difference learning and has become influential in theories linking prediction, cognitive maps, and hippocampal representations.

The key intuition is that an SR encodes predictive relationships: “from here, what tends to happen next (and after that)?” This can look like memory because it preserves structured expectations about sequences, without storing a verbatim episodic history. Cognitive extensions connect SR to temporal context ideas, explicitly tying predictive state representations to how context evolves over time in memory models.

Where Markov models fit, and where they break

Fits well:

  • Event-state inference: When experience can be usefully segmented into latent “modes” or “events,” HMM-like formalisms offer a compact modeling language.
  • Predictive structure: SR formalizes how agents can store predictive structure about environments using Markov dynamics.
  • Mathematical tractability: Stationarity, recurrence, ergodicity, and mixing provide well-developed tools for analyzing long-run behavior and sensitivity to perturbations.

Breaks (or needs augmentation):

  • Rich autobiographical memory: Episodic recall can depend on multi-scale history, goals, and schemas. A first-order Markov state is usually too small.
  • Non-stationarity: Humans learn; transition rules change with experience. A stationary transition matrix can be a poor assumption.
  • Long-range dependencies: When distant past affects the future even after conditioning on the present (because the present state is underspecified), higher-order or hierarchical models are needed.

Practical modeling moves

  • State augmentation: Add variables for context, goal, uncertainty, or running summaries so the Markov assumption becomes more plausible.
  • Hierarchy: Use multi-timescale states (fast sensory; slower event; slower schema) rather than a single flat chain.
  • Latent-state inference: Prefer HMM/state-space approaches when the “state” is not directly observable but must be inferred.
  • Interpret with care: “Memoryless” is a statement about conditional independence, not a claim that the system has no stored information.
